newsitem.title: YUGOSLAVIA: Serbian bankers say NBY debt moves not enough.
newsitem.headline: Serbian bankers say NBY debt moves not enough.

text.p: Serbian bankers criticised on Thursday central bank plans to reschedule part of their bad-debt portfolio until January 31, saying the move would not cure the problem.
The National Bank of Yugoslavia (NBY) said earlier it would offer credit relief to state and commercial banks by converting all credits given to them into securities.

Central bank vice-governor Ratko Banovic said credits given to the state would be converted to state bonds, funds extended to public companies would convert into bonds and commercial banks' borrowing would be exchanged for honoured drafts without limits.

In an attempt to close down the bad-debt saga, NBY said in the latest issue of the Official Gazette that it would reschedule matured commercial banks' debt to the NBY and delay payment until January 31, 1997.
The extension of the deadline will give bankers time to prepare to issue securities to be traded on the local market.
"We talk about 1.976 billion dinars ($387 million) in bad debt to be converted into short-term securities," Serbian deputy finance minister Garib Hadzini told a bankers meeting.
Hadzini said it would have been a fatal blow for insolvent commercial banks if they were to pay all matured debt at once by December 15 as originally planned.
He said the conversion programme was nearly finished and it only remained to determine the interest rate.
Hadzini said the latest NBY decision to reschedule matured debt leads temporarily to improved liquidity of the banking and enterprise sector.
But bankers called on NBY to include the state and public companies' debt in the conversion scenario.
"If not, this conversion of our debt only means a delay in payment for us and substantially improves the central bank's credit portfolio," said Vitomir Janjuz, director of the Kreditna Banka Beograd.
Biljana Seskar of the Yugoslav Banking Association (YBA) said banks managed to collect only around 352 million dinars from troubled debtors.
According to YBA statistics, banks had to write off two billion dinars at the end of September and were expected to do the same with another 2.6 billion when the debt matures.

Svetozar Rikanovic, former Yugoslav finance minister and now a consultant with the private economic research institute CES-Mecon, welcomed the NBY effort to securitise the bad debt but asked whether the central bank could guarantee the successful outcome of the programme.
"We need instruments of sufficient quality to enter our financial market, not bad paper that would lead to disaster at the very beginning of its development," Rikanovic said.

Milomir Spasic of Slavija Banka questioned attempts to convert companies' bad debt to securities. "How can a company issue a bond or any other security and guarantee for it, if it does not service its current debt" he said.
